Description:

The bronze sculpture Salome by Swedish artist Anders Jönsson presents the biblical figure in a poised, almost meditative moment rather than in overt drama. Kneeling on one leg with the other extended behind, Salome holds the head of John the Baptist in a shallow dish, her body balanced between movement and stillness. The simplified, rhythmic modeling of the figure, together with the flowing drapery over her knee, reflects the sculptural language of Nordic classicism from the early 20th century.

Jönsson’s handling of bronze, with its rich green-brown patina, gives the surface a tactile depth that enhances the solemn mood of the scene. The work is signed by the artist and bears the foundry mark of Otto Meyers Eftr., underscoring its quality of execution. This Salome is an evocative example of Swedish figurative sculpture, where mythic subject matter, refined proportions and timeless material come together in a quietly powerful work.

Description:

This vintage wooden sculpture by Johnny Mattsson is a distilled example of Swedish modernism within the broader tradition of Scandinavian design. Carved in Sweden during the 1950s, the work rises from a dark, cubic plinth into a tall, tapering form with a sharply pointed tip. A precisely hollowed inner curve defines the front of the piece, revealing the fine grain of the wood and creating a play of light and shadow along the surface. The sculpture is signed “JM” on the underside of the base, confirming its authorship.

Mattsson, known for his mastery of wood and interest in abstract, biomorphic forms, achieves here a remarkable clarity of expression: purity of line, exquisite craftsmanship and a quiet, contemplative character. The restrained geometry and subtle asymmetry connect the work to the ideals of vintage Scandinavian design in the post-war period, where natural materials and hand craftsmanship were used to explore modern, sculptural forms. As an authentic mid-century piece, it offers a concise, beautifully realised document of Scandinavian design thinking at the height of Swedish modernism.

description:

Measurements:

L: 49 cm / 19 1/3’’

Description:

Rune Hagberg (1924 - 2015) was a self-taught pupil of Zen Buddhism who explored silence and introspection within his work.

Born in Uppsala, Sweden, Hagberg became heavily influenced by Eastern calligraphy throughout his life – and developed a spontaneous sign painting style with a strong concentration on a select amount of characters rooted in Zen Buddhism. His informal meditative practice found its place between concretism and expressionism which was widespread in the 1950s. Later in his life, these symbols would be bound into reels and tied together with string - white, ascetic, and secretive within their frames.

Eventually, Hagberg's practice came to focus on a gradual loosening of the picture surface, a kind of elimination of the sheet of paper, as if to approach the idea of nothingness. This exploration later found expression in sculptural objects. His oeuvre of ink painting turned him into a public figure in Sweden – hosting a long series of exhibitions, most notably at Moderna Museet in Malmö and Norrköping Art Museum. He also exhibited abroad in Japan in 1955 alongside a group of Eastern painters and calligraphers.

Signed.

Provenance:

The Estate of Rune Hagberg

Description:

This framed sculptural work, titled Blåsegel, was created in 1983 by the Swedish artist Stig Åke Lund. Constructed as a shallow relief, the piece combines layered elements into a compact, architectural composition that sits between sculpture and collage.

Lund drew much of his visual language from nature, distilling organic motifs into simplified, botanical shapes. Throughout his career, Lund worked fluently across a wide range of media, including metal, wood, graphic techniques, and sculptural assemblage. His reliefs and montages often blur the boundary between image and object, inviting the viewer to read the work both as a composition and as a physical construction.

Stig Åke Lund’s work is held in several important public collections, underscoring his international recognition. Institutions such as The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm include his works, situating Blåsegel within a broader body of refined Scandinavian mid century art.

Description:

This sculptural work, titled Rabarberblad (Rhubarb Leaf), was created by Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd in the 1950s and cast in patinated bronze. The piece captures the organic form of a single leaf with striking naturalism, preserving the veining, folds, and subtle irregularities of the plant.

The sculpture was produced in a limited, numbered edition, typically comprising around twenty casts. While the overall form remains consistent across the series, each example is distinguished by slight variations in the green-brown patination, resulting from the individual finishing process. These tonal differences give each leaf its own character and surface expression, underscoring the uniqueness of each numbered cast within the edition.

Carl Fredrik Reuterswärd was born in Stockholm in 1934 and became one of Sweden’s most internationally recognised artists. He played a significant role in the development of the modern art scene in Sweden, particularly during the dynamic cultural period surrounding the early years of Moderna Museet in Stockholm. Although he is widely known worldwide for the iconic peace sculpture Non-Violence—the knotted revolver installed at sites including the United Nations headquarters in New York—his earlier sculptural works reveal a deep engagement with form and material.

Description:

This sculptural bowl titled Il passagio – liten (The Passage – small) was designed by Inger Sannes in 2014 and carved from white marble. The surface retains a distinctly tactile, almost geological quality, with rhythmically worked grooves that reveal both the resistance of the stone and the physical intensity of the carving process. Despite its weight and material density, the form appears open and poised, balancing mass with an unexpected sense of lightness.

The work belongs to Sannes’ ongoing exploration of transition and transformation. A recurring idea in her practice is the dialogue between what is grounded and what is in motion: one element rooted and stable, the other pushing outward, suggesting growth, departure, or a shift in direction.

Inger Sannes works between Stockholm and Pietrasanta, Italy, where she has access to the same marble traditions that shaped classical sculpture. Alongside her smaller works, she has realised major public commissions, including a large-scale version of Il Passaggio for Frösunda Kyrka in Gnesta, Sweden.

Description:

This mixed-media relief by Zbigniew Stanley Kupczynski belongs to a decisive moment in the artist’s career, when he moved beyond painting and began working sculpturally with metal in the late 1960s. The front presents a dense, abstract composition built from layered metal fragments, marked by perforations, hammered textures and tonal variation that give the surface a strong physical presence. The reverse side reveals an integrated collage of period newspapers, photographic reproductions and the artist’s signature, reinforcing the work’s dual nature as both object and document.

Kupczynski’s use of industrial materials during this period reflects a broader shift in his practice, as he explored new ways of translating expressionist concerns into relief and construction. These metal works were exhibited across Poland, Sweden and Denmark and stand apart from his more widely known painted portraits and abstractions. The combination of raw material, historical ephemera and hand-worked surfaces situates the piece firmly within the experimental spirit of post-war European art.

Born in 1928, Zbigniew Kupczynski developed an international career from the 1950s onward, exhibiting extensively across Europe, North America, Australia and Japan. His work gained early recognition during a politically complex era, including notable acquisitions by prominent figures, and this relief captures a pivotal transitional phase as his reputation expanded beyond painting into sculptural and mixed-media expression.

This sculptural wood relief titled Vågen (The Wave), created by Elli Hemberg during the 1960s, is composed of intersecting wooden elements arranged in a layered, dynamic structure. Built from overlapping beams set at varying angles, the composition creates a sense of movement and tension across the surface. Through the careful arrangement of these structural elements, Hemberg transforms solid wood into a rhythmic composition that suggests shifting motion.

The work reflects Hemberg’s interest in what she described as “dynamic symmetry,” where repeated forms generate visual rhythm and spatial balance. The interlocking beams evoke the rising and falling energy of water, while the rough texture and visible construction highlight the material character of the wood.

Elli Hemberg (1896–1994) was a Swedish abstract painter and sculptor known particularly for her architectural sculptures and many of her larger works were commissioned for public buildings, reflecting the modernist ambition to integrate art into architecture and everyday environments. Description:

Hugo Liisberg (1896–1958) was a Danish sculptor and ceramicist celebrated for his dynamic depictions of the animal kingdom, where naturalistic observation meets dramatic tension. This bronze sculpture of an eagle striking a swan exemplifies his ability to capture the raw vitality of nature in motion. The raised wings and twisting bodies convey both elegance and struggle, a theme Liisberg often explored in his public commissions such as Ørnebrønden in Silkeborg 1931 and De vilde svaner in Odense 1951.

Executed with a rich, green-brown patina, the work reveals Liisberg’s sculptural precision and sensitivity to surface texture, hallmarks of his practice that extended from monumental public works to smaller bronzes and ceramic figures produced for Royal Copenhagen and Saxbo. This piece reflects his enduring fascination with birds and the dramatic interplay between predator and prey, offering a powerful study of movement and form.

Liisberg’s artistic significance is underscored by his presence in major museum collections, including Vejen Kunstmuseum, Museum Sønderjylland, Trapholt, Statens Museum for Kunst, KØS – Museum for kunst i det offentlige rum, ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum, and Esbjerg Kunstmuseum.
